lead: A fluid is a substance that flows: it cannot hold a fixed shape and cannot resist a shear force when at rest. Real fluids are made of molecules in constant motion, with empty space between them. Engineers avoid tracking every molecule. When the region of interest is much larger than the mean free path (which is itself much larger than the molecular spacing in a gas), we replace the crowd of molecules with a smooth continuous medium, a continuum, and speak of properties at a point. The same idea lets us sort fluids into ideal models (no viscosity) and real fluids (viscosity present).
prereq: You need only school physics: force, area, and the fact that matter is made of molecules.

blocks.text: A fluid is a substance that cannot resist a shear force when at rest: put a shear on it and it keeps deforming. Gases and liquids both do this.

At the molecular scale a fluid is mostly empty space. In air at 20 °C and 1 atm, a molecule travels on average about 6.8×10⁻⁸ m between collisions. This distance is the mean free path, written λ. In a liquid the molecules are packed much closer, so λ is of the order of the molecular spacing, about 10⁻¹⁰ m.
The body length L is the smallest length over which you need the answer: the diameter of a sensor opening, the gap in a valve, the width of a microchannel.

The ratio λ/L decides whether the continuum idea works. If λ/L is very small, a molecule collides with other molecules far more often than it crosses the body, so the crowd behaves like a smooth medium. If λ/L is not small, molecules cross the body without colliding and the continuum fails. Some syllabi write Kn = λ/L and call it the Knudsen number.

blocks.where: λ is the mean free path (m), the average distance a molecule travels between collisions; L is the smallest body length of interest (m); Kn is the Knudsen number, dimensionless.

items: Find λ for the gas from its pressure and temperature.
Find L, the smallest length in the problem.
Treat the fluid as a continuum if Kn is below about 0.01. Above about 0.1, use rarefied-gas methods.

sections.h3: The averaging volume and the continuum point

blocks.text: A continuum point means a small volume, not a mathematical point. Pick a point P in the fluid. Draw a small volume ΔV around P. Average the mass of the molecules inside, and divide by ΔV to get a density. Now shrink ΔV. While ΔV is still large compared with the molecular spacing, the average mass divided by ΔV stays steady — this steady value is the density at P. Only when ΔV shrinks to the averaging volume, small enough that individual molecules entering and leaving start to matter, does the value start to jump about. Use the steady plateau value as the property at P; the smallest volume that still sits on the plateau is the averaging volume.
The averaging volume contains many molecules, yet it is tiny compared with the body. For air at ordinary conditions, a cube of side 1 μm holds about 2.5×10⁷ molecules, enough for a smooth average.

Once every point has a property, you can write density as ρ(x, y, z, t) and pressure as p(x, y, z, t). These are field variables. Calculus then applies, and you can differentiate and integrate them. This is the whole reason the continuum is useful: it turns a problem about 10²³ molecules into a problem about a few smooth functions.

An ideal fluid is a model with viscosity μ = 0. It cannot support a shear stress, even when moving. It is also taken as incompressible (constant density) and without surface tension. Some syllabi call an ideal fluid inviscid. An ideal fluid is not a fluid with zero density; it has mass and inertia.

A real fluid has μ > 0. It resists shear, and Newton's law of viscosity links shear stress to velocity gradient (see 1.3). Real liquids also have surface tension (see 1.5), and real fluids are compressible to some degree.

Why keep the ideal model? Because it makes the mathematics simple. Bernoulli's equation and potential flow assume an ideal fluid; over short distances and at low viscosity, water and air follow those results closely. The difference appears in pipe friction, drag, and pump losses, which are real-fluid effects (see Unit 4, Viscous Flow Through Pipes).

spec.title: Continuum idea and fluid models
spec.aria: Molecules are averaged into a continuum point, which can be modelled as an ideal fluid with zero viscosity or a real fluid with viscosity.

examples.question: A pressure sensor has a circular opening of diameter 1 mm. Air at 20 °C and 1 atm has mean free path λ = 6.8×10⁻⁸ m. Compare the opening with the mean free path, compute the Knudsen number, and decide whether the air behaves as a continuum at the sensor scale.
steps: Record the data: opening diameter D = 1 mm = 1×10⁻³ m; mean free path λ = 6.8×10⁻⁸ m.
Compare the opening with the mean free path: L/λ = 1×10⁻³ / 6.8×10⁻⁸.
Convert to the usual Knudsen number: Kn = λ/L = 1 / (L/λ) = 6.8×10⁻⁵.
Compare with the continuum threshold: Kn = 6.8×10⁻⁵ is far below 0.01, equivalently L/λ ≫ 100.
Conclusion: the air is a continuum at the sensor opening.
examples.answer: L/λ ≈ 1.47×10⁴ and Kn ≈ 6.8×10⁻⁵; because Kn ≪ 0.01, the air behaves as a continuum at the 1 mm sensor opening.

traps: Ideal fluid is not zero density. Ideal means μ = 0 and usually incompressible. It still has mass, weight and inertia.
Ideal fluid and ideal gas are different models. An ideal gas obeys pV = nRT and can have viscosity.
The continuum is a length-scale assumption, not a universal truth. A 1 mm sensor in air sees a continuum; a 100 nm channel in the same air does not.
Mean free path λ changes with pressure. At fixed temperature λ ∝ 1/p. Do not use the sea-level value at 10 km altitude.
Unit slip in Kn: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m and 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m. Kn is dimensionless; do not write it as 0.01 m.

quiz.q: Define a fluid in one sentence.
quiz.a: A fluid is a substance that deforms continuously when a shear stress acts on it and cannot resist shear at rest.

quiz.q: What is the mean free path?
quiz.a: The average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions, written λ, with unit metre.

quiz.q: Why does the continuum assumption fail for air at very high altitude?
quiz.a: At low pressure λ grows as 1/p at fixed temperature. For a fixed body length L, Kn = λ/L rises. Above Kn ≈ 0.01 the molecules cross the body without colliding enough to form a smooth average, so the continuum model breaks down.

quiz.q: Distinguish an ideal fluid from an ideal gas.
quiz.a: An ideal fluid is a model with zero viscosity and usually constant density. An ideal gas is a gas that obeys pV = nRT; it has mass and can be viscous. Air can be an ideal gas and a real fluid at the same time.

quiz.q: Air has λ = 1.0×10⁻⁷ m. A microchannel is 2 μm wide. Compute Kn. Is the continuum valid?
quiz.a: L = 2 μm = 2×10⁻⁶ m. Kn = λ/L = 1.0×10⁻⁷ / 2×10⁻⁶ = 0.05. Kn is above 0.01, so the continuum is not strictly valid; rarefied-gas effects matter.

quiz.q: A pressure tap has diameter 0.5 mm. Air has λ = 6.8×10⁻⁸ m. Compute L/λ and Kn.
quiz.a: L = 5×10⁻⁴ m. L/λ = 5×10⁻⁴ / 6.8×10⁻⁸ ≈ 7.35×10³. Kn = λ/L ≈ 1.36×10⁻⁴. Kn ≪ 0.01, so the continuum is valid.

quiz.q: A student writes: 'An ideal fluid has zero density, so it has no inertia.' Identify the error and state what an ideal fluid really is.
quiz.a: The error is equating ideal with massless. An ideal fluid has μ = 0 and is usually taken incompressible; its density is nonzero, so it has inertia. Zero density would make pressure forces meaningless because ρ appears in Bernoulli's equation.

quiz.q: Why can a manometer use pressure 'at a point' when the liquid is made of molecules?
quiz.a: The manometer tube is much larger than the molecular spacing. The averaging volume contains many molecules and is small compared with the tube, so pressure is a smooth field variable. The continuum limit gives the same pressure at the same level on both limbs (see 1.7).

beyond: Not for the exam. The Knudsen number controls rarefied gas dynamics in vacuum systems, high-altitude flight and micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS). Above Kn ≈ 0.1 engineers use the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method instead of the Navier–Stokes equations. Microfluidic devices with channels a few micrometres wide routinely sit in the slip-flow regime. Search 'Knudsen number rarefied gas' or 'continuum breakdown microchannel' to go further.
